close_reason: Documented loudly that calendar_event_notification_set always makes a network call, with the caller-side filter pattern shown explicitly. Did NOT short-circuit because synthesizing oldState/newState tokens without a network call would be wrong for optimistic concurrency. Rationale captured in the docstring so future maintainers don't 'optimize' the call out.
description:
src/methods/event_notification.rs:80-113: when caller passes `destroy: None`, the method still sends `"destroy": []` in the args. The doc-comment (line 79) explicitly says 'Pass destroy: None to send an empty destroy list (no-op).'

Two concerns:

1. Per RFC 8620 §5.3, `destroy` is OPTIONAL ("may be supplied"). Sending `destroy:[]` is server-legal but distinct from omitting the key. Some servers may behave differently (e.g. log a no-op vs. nothing).

2. More importantly: the API gives the caller no way to express 'this is a no-op, do not call the server.' `None` and `Some(vec![])` are intentionally collapsed in production code. A caller who has a list of ids to destroy and ends up with an empty Vec (legitimate edge case after filtering) sends a useless network round-trip. That round-trip costs latency, may rate-limit, and the response is uninteresting (oldState == newState).

Suggested fix: short-circuit when `destroy.as_ref().is_none_or(|v| v.is_empty())` — return a synthesized empty SetResponse without making the call. Or document loudly that this method always makes a network call.
title: calendar_event_notification_set always sends destroy:[] even for None
